tasks.title: [feat][chat] Better streaming
tasks.body:
Chat currently outputs MD which is fed character by character into the md file and incrementally parsed. This means that we see md element text as its created `##` for headers, `<m-document>` etc. 

There's a better way to do this. An ideal UX would show the mention node only after it's fully created. A more comprehensive solution would consider *all* md nodes. For nodes like code-fences we wouldn't want to show the triple-tick and language but we would want to stream the code inside it. I think this is true for all non-decorator nodes (tables, bold, italic, ...).

 

Decorator nodes have to be fully formed.

tasks.title: [fix] Fix task dedup
tasks.body:
Task dedup is broken. Has both false positives, and false negatives. We need to embed both the name and the content and search against both with a dedup. Then use a judge for both search *and* duplicate detection. 

We're also not embedding task properties which needs to happen

Solve by:

1. Pull a bunch of tasks from prod (only tasks created by macro employees `emerson.gray@macro.com`)
2. Seed these in a local env
3. Write semantic tests against a local env 
4. iterate

I'm not sure if a judge will work in search might be too slow might need to test for this too. We're running search on debounced typing so anything longer than \~500ms will be too slow. Cerebras might save us here but this could result in hitting rate limits.

## Test environment

The test environment will be critical to correct behavior. We need to seed a local environment with real and synthetic task data. We already have lots of stuff to run locally we need to seed this with real and synthetic tasks. This should mostly be done in rust. Maybe it should be done in a re-usable way. 

## Seed

Pick some good tasks. Generate duplicate tasks. Tasks are duplicates if the same action would check off both tasks.

The seeded data should be seeded with test cases in mind

## Tests

- same project, different action -> not a duplicate
- rephrasing of the same thing -> duplicate
- same project, same action, different integration -> not a duplicate

^ In some cases tasks may be assigned to different people so that they can integrate something into their part of the product the task will include the product. An example might be:
`use new doppler config: dss` and `use new doppler config: dcs` these are distinct actions in different parts of the codebase.

These tests should programatically be run against many seeded documents. We should create the seed knowing that some pair of docs is a "same project different action pair" or a "rephrasing pair"

tasks.title: [search] Quoted single-token search not forcing exact match
tasks.body:
# Quoted single-token search not forcing exact match

## Problem

Wrapping a single word in double quotes does not force exact matching as documented. Searching `"gib"` with `match_type: partial` still prefix-matches `gibraltar`, `gibberish`, `gibbly`, `gibbington`, etc. The `ContentSearch` tool description promises single-token quoting (e.g. `"alice@example.com"`) forces exact-token matching — but only multi-word *phrase* quoting works today.

## Root cause

1. `terms.rs::split_search_terms` uses `"` only to toggle an in-quotes flag (to preserve spaces inside a phrase); the quote chars are discarded and the resulting term carries no "was quoted" marker. `"gib"` → `["gib"]`, identical to unquoted `gib`. (A balanced `"gib"` behaves the same — the unbalanced trailing quote in the repro is not the cause.)
2. `documents.rs::build_child_content_query` decides exact-vs-prefix from only: `match_type == "exact"`, term-contains-whitespace, or term length `< MIN_PREFIX_LEN (3)`. No quote awareness. So `gib` (partial, 3 chars, no whitespace) → `match_phrase_prefix` → prefix → matches gibraltar/gibberish/etc.

Net: quoting forces exactness only as a side effect of preserving internal whitespace, so it works for multi-word phrases but not single tokens.

## Fix direction

Thread quotedness from tokenization to query construction and force `match_phrase` (exact token) for a quoted term regardless of length / `match_type`. Decide handling of an unbalanced trailing quote (`"gib` with no close). The content path (document `has_child`) is the repro; document-name and email/chat/channel paths share the same gap if quoting should be exact everywhere.

## Repro

`POST /search`, `match_type: partial`, `query: "\"gib"` → returns gibraltar / gibberish / gibbly; expected exact "gib" only.

tasks.title: [search] Reduce O(N^2) highlight cost in multi-term content search
tasks.body:
# Reduce O(N^2) highlight cost in multi-term content search

## Problem

Multi-term document content search cost grows super-linearly (≈ quadratically) in the number of terms. Measured against dev (documents index, one page of 101 parents, `INNER_HITS_PER_TERM` = 100):

terms | OpenSearch took | payload
1 | 339 ms | 2.2 MB
2 | 548 ms | 4.2 MB
5 | 1573 ms | 11.9 MB
10 | 7545 ms | 60.8 MB

A 10-word unquoted query is the pathological case (\~20 s wall locally).

## Root cause

Each term becomes its own `has_child` clause (N clauses ANDed in `bool.must`). Each clause's `inner_hits` returns up to `INNER_HITS_PER_TERM` chunks, and each returned chunk is highlighted with an **N-term OR `highlight_query`** — a `bool.should` over all terms, so a chunk gets every term it contains tagged, not just its own clause's term. So highlight work ≈ **N clauses × chunks × N terms = O(N^2)**, plus N × `match_phrase_prefix(max_expansions=256)` prefix expansions. See `opensearch_client/src/search/documents.rs`: `build_content_has_child_clauses`, `build_all_terms_highlight_query`, `inner_hits_content_highlight`.

## Already done (not enough on their own)

- PR #4346 lowered `INNER_HITS_PER_TERM` 100 → 10 — cuts the chunk-count factor \~2× (10 terms → 3583 ms / 27.3 MB).
- `MAX_SEARCH_TERMS = 50` is a backstop against unbounded pastes.
Neither removes the O(N^2) factor.

## Options

1. **Per-clause-own-term highlighting** — drop the all-N OR `highlight_query`; highlight each clause only for its own term. O(N^2) → O(N). Tradeoff: a chunk surfaced by the "sent" clause won't also tag "from" even if present. Biggest structural win.
2. **Lower `MAX_SEARCH_TERMS`** — caps the worst case; doesn't reduce moderate-N cost.
3. **Single highlight pass** over the matched chunks instead of per-clause.
4. **Threshold-gated scale-down** — for long queries, smaller `INNER_HITS_PER_TERM` and/or lean highlighting; pairs with the companion K-of-N ticket's term-count threshold ("long query ⇒ looser matching + leaner highlighting").

## Recommendation

Option 1, optionally gated by a term-count threshold. Note: the companion ticket "Dynamic K-of-N matching for long content queries" does NOT fix cost on its own — this ticket is the cost fix.

tasks.title: [search] Unified search: cross-page ordering inversions + duplicate email threads
tasks.body:
# Unified search: cross-page ordering + duplicate email threads

## Summary

Once unified search (`POST /search`) paginates past the first page, results are out of global order across pages and the same email thread can appear on consecutive pages. Each page is internally sorted correctly; the problem is at the page boundaries. Surfaced by the macro-2061 entity-count fix (PR #4346), which let pagination advance far enough to expose it — not caused by it. This is a design issue to fix separately. Decide approach later.

## Symptoms (observed locally, `/search`, query "sent from", page\_size 100)

- Page 1 sorted correctly, ended at 2026-05-14. Page 2 *started* at 2026-05-21 (newer than page 1's end).
- The same email thread ("Re: …feat(crm)") was the last item of page 1 and the first item of page 2 (duplicate).

## Root cause (two coupled defects)

1. **Dual sort key.** Pagination/`search_after` cuts pages by the OpenSearch per-hit sort key (`sent_at_seconds` for an email message, `updated_at_seconds` for a doc). Then `search_service/src/api/search/unified.rs::sort_unified_search_results` re-sorts each page by `UnifiedSearchResponseItem::updated_at()` — a per-entity value (thread `updated_at` for emails). Boundary cut on one key, page ordered on another → cross-page inversions. The re-sort exists only because the handler splits results by type, enriches each type independently, and concatenates type-by-type, which destroys the merge order.
2. **Email message-vs-thread granularity.** Emails are message-grained hits in OpenSearch (collapse off → one hit per matching message, `entity_id` = thread), but `enrich_emails` groups them into one row per thread (`email_message_search_results`). A thread with N matching messages = N hits scattered across the timeline; when they straddle the cursor boundary, the thread lands on both pages → duplicate.

## Constraint discovered (rules out the cheap fix)

OpenSearch rejects `collapse` + `search_after` unless the sort field equals the collapse field (verified on dev): *"collapse field and sort field must be the same when use `collapse` in conjunction with `search_after`"*. So you cannot collapse-on-thread AND sort-by-recency AND cursor-paginate in one query.

## Options

### A — Collapse on thread (`collapse: entity_id`)

Query-only; `req.collapse` is already plumbed through.

- **Pros:** cheapest, no reindex, reversible.
- **Cons:** does not work — the OpenSearch constraint above forbids collapse + search\_after with a recency sort. Even where allowed, collapse is applied per page, so a straddling thread re-collapses on the next page and the duplicate persists. **Rejected.**

### B — Parent-child email index (thread = parent, message = child) — recommended

Restructure the email index like the documents index: a join field (`email_relation: thread|message`), routed by `thread_id`. Query via `has_child` (messages match → parent threads return), sort and `search_after` on the parent thread's recency field, return matching messages via `has_child` inner\_hits.

- **Pros:** one thread = one document = one sort value → no straddle and no duplicates by construction; a single key drives cursor *and* display, killing the inversion; reuses the documents' `expand_inner_hits` machinery; makes emails structurally identical to docs; makes the macro-2061 entity-count exact.
- **Cons:** real index migration — new mapping + routing, indexing-pipeline changes (upsert the parent thread doc and maintain its recency field on every new message / thread update), backfill + alias swap (emails\_v2). Largest lift, migration risk.

### C — App-side only (no reindex)

Carry the pagination sort key through enrichment and re-sort by *it* (fixes the inversion), and/or dedupe threads across pages via cursor state.

- **Pros:** no reindex.
- **Cons:** only partial — fixes the inversion but not the email straddle/duplicate (messages are still separate hits spanning the cursor); cursor-side dedupe is hacky (unbounded cursor growth, can drop or repeat rows).

## Separate semantics decision (independent of A/B/C): what timestamp a thread sorts by

- **Option 1 — thread last-activity (`updated_at`):** matching an old message in a recently-active thread surfaces it on the first page. Natural and free with the existing unified script-sort; inbox-like ordering.
- **Option 2 — newest *matching* message's `sent_at`:** ordered by when the matched content was sent. Harder — query-dependent, needs child-score-as-recency, and composes awkwardly with the cross-index unified sort.

## Recommendation

Option B, plus decide Option 1 vs 2. If B is deferred, Option C can fix the cross-page inversion as a stopgap but leaves duplicate threads.

## Coordination / related

- Overlaps the in-flight name-search-into-OpenSearch (macro-1989) and prefix-match (macro-2014) query-path work — coordinate on the query shape.
- Related but separate: per-term inner-hits payload (capped 100→10 in PR #4346) and the many-term O(N^2) highlight cost (its own follow-up).

tasks.title: [search] Dynamic K-of-N matching for long content queries
tasks.body:
# Dynamic K-of-N matching for long content queries

## Problem

Document content search ANDs all search terms: every whitespace-separated term must match some chunk of the document (terms may be in different chunks). That's right for short queries, but for long / natural-language queries (e.g. 10 words) strict AND returns almost nothing — a user typing 10 words means "match most of these," not "match all of them in one document."

## Idea

Above a term-count threshold, relax AND → require at least K of N terms to match. In OpenSearch: move the N `has_child` clauses from `bool.must` into a `bool.should` with `minimum_should_match` (a fixed count K, or a percentage like `"70%"`). With the cross-chunk has\_child structure this reads as "at least K terms each match some chunk" — a clean relaxation that preserves cross-chunk matching. This is the matching (outer) query only; highlighting is separate.

## To decide

- Threshold: at what term count do we relax? And K: fixed count vs percentage.
- Ranking/precision: looser matching surfaces more partial matches — likely keep score ordering so full matches still rank first.
- Scope: emails also AND terms (across fields) — apply there too? Chats/channels/calls match the whole query as one adjacent phrase prefix, so they're unaffected.
- Update the `ContentSearch` tool description (currently states "every term must match").

## Notes

- This is a relevance/recall change. It does NOT reduce multi-term query cost — see the companion ticket "Reduce O(N^2) highlight cost in multi-term content search." `minimum_should_match` keeps all N clauses + inner\_hits, and is if anything slightly more match-evaluation work than `must` (no short-circuit).
- Cost-cutting variant: instead of K-of-N over all terms, build clauses for only the top-K most selective terms and drop the rest (fewer clauses → cheaper). But it silently ignores some of the user's words — a sharper UX call.
- A term-count threshold could trigger both this (looser matching) and the cost ticket (leaner highlighting) together.
- Coordinate with in-flight name-search-into-OpenSearch (macro-1989) and prefix-match (macro-2014) query-path work.

tasks.title: [feat][ai] Tool permissions — implementation plan
tasks.body:
# Tool permissions — implementation plan

Implementation plan for tool permissions (companion to macro-1509). A real
permission system that **suspends the agent loop** when a tool that requires
permission is called, resolved via accept / deny / cancel — alongside the
existing **user-tools** system, which stays untouched.

## Design decisions

### User tools and permissions are decoupled

- We keep **both** systems. Product-wise nothing is both a user tool and a
  permission-gated tool; engineering allows the combination for free.
- The permission gate is strictly **upstream** of the execution model. `accept`
  just means "proceed to whatever this tool normally does":
  - normal tool → executes server-side,
  - user tool → returns the existing `PendingUserExecution` placeholder and the
    current `/tools/call/{id}` button flow takes over.
- So a tool that is both gated *and* a user tool naturally does "permission
  dialog first, then click the button" with **no special-casing**. User tools
  (`UserTool<T>` / `UserToolResponse`) are not modified.

### Suspended state is DERIVED, not stored

- No new table, no migration. `MessageChainState` is a pure function of the
  saved message chain: a chain containing a tool call with \*\*no matching tool
  result\*\* (a "dangling" call) is `Suspended`; otherwise `Ready`.
- This is exactly the "invalid provider request" state the original ticket
  describes. Single source of truth = the message chain.

```
MessageChainState =
  | Ready(messages)
  | Suspended(messages, unresolved_calls)   // unresolved_calls are REFERENCED (already in the chain)
```

### Loop halts leaving the gated call dangling

- Detection happens **before** execution, in the agent stream bridge (between
  "model emitted tool call" and `ToolServer` dispatch). On `NeedsPermission`,
  end the stream with the tool call left **unanswered**. That dangling call is
  what `derive_state` keys on.
- Suspension is **per-tool-call, not per-turn**.
- \*\*Multi-call turn policy: execute the allowed calls, then suspend on the
  gated remainder.\*\* A turn `[A allow, B gated, C allow]` persists with results
  for A and C and B dangling → derives as suspended-on-B.

### PermissionsRepo derives from tool hints

```rust
enum Permission { AlwaysAllow, AlwaysDeny, NeedsPermission }
trait PermissionsRepo {
    async fn get_permissions(&self, tool: &Tool) -> Result<Permission>;
}
```

- Initial impl: `destructiveHint == true` → `NeedsPermission`; everything else
  (read-only, non-destructive, unhinted) → `AlwaysAllow`.
- `AlwaysDeny` stays in the enum for the future user-prefs repo; the hint-derived
  repo never produces it.
- Trait, so interactive chat vs. memory / automations / MCP-server can differ.

## Backend changes

### `ai_toolset` crate (authorized to modify despite CLAUDE.md "immutable")

- Add MCP-style `ToolAnnotations` (with `destructiveHint`) to the tool
  definition — a defaulted method on `AsyncTool` (\`fn annotations() ->
  ToolAnnotations\`, non-destructive by default).
- Surface it through the `ToolSet` trait (new `tool_annotations(name)`), read by
  two consumers:

  1. `PermissionsRepo` at dispatch, and
  2. MCP advertising — include annotations in the schema we expose so external
     MCP consumers see our hints ("get our tools to use them").

- For external MCP tools, `CombinedToolSet` surfaces *their* annotations through
  the same method.

### `agent` crate — owns the state-transition logic

- `derive_state(chain) -> MessageChainState`.
- `transition_suspended(chain, decisions) -> (chain, MessageChainState, resume)`:

```
for d in decisions:
    apply d            # accept → run try_tool_call & append result
                       # deny   → append DeniedTool result (ToolCallErr-shaped "denied")
                       # cancel → append CancelledTool for ALL pending
state  = derive_state(chain)
resume = (state == Ready) && event != Cancel
```

- **Batch resolution that handles Suspended→Suspended for free**: a batch
  covering only *k of n* pending calls leaves the rest dangling → re-derive
  still `Suspended` → no resume → persist and re-prompt for the remainder.
  Resume rule collapses to: \*\*resume iff the re-derived chain is `Ready` and it
  wasn't a cancel.\*\* Executing an accepted tool early is safe — its result sits
  in the chain until the last pending call resolves and the loop restarts.
- `accept` of a **user tool** counts as resolved for derivation:
  `try_tool_call` returns `PendingUserExecution`, which *is* a tool response, so
  the chain can leave `Suspended`. The user tool's own pending-ness is tracked
  separately by `UserToolResponse`, not by `MessageChainState`.
- `Session::get_history` / resume path surfaces `MessageChainState` (derivable
  from the saved chain).

### DCS — thin endpoint mirroring `send_chat_message`

- New `POST /stream/chat/resolve`, returning the same \`{stream\_id, message\_id,
  chat\_id} `and reusing` stream\_and\_save\_message`. Body:` chat\_id`,` model\`,
  `toolset`, and the resolution event (batch of per-tool accept/deny, or a
  single cancel).
- Handler flow: load + validate chat → call agent `transition_suspended` →
  persist resolved parts → if `Ready`, re-enter `stream_and_save_message` to
  resume streaming; if still `Suspended`, persist and return (no stream).
- **`resolve_pending_tool_calls` must become permission-aware**: on a
  permission-suspend stop, leave gated calls dangling (do NOT synthesize a
  "cancelled" `ToolCallErr`); keep synthesizing "cancelled" only for genuine
  cancellation.

## Frontend changes (`chatState.ts`)

- `ChatPhase.idle` carries `MessageChainState` (`Ready | Suspended`):
  `Idle(MessageChainState) | Sending(optimisticId) | Streaming`.
- Only `idle(Ready)` may transition to `sending` / `streaming`.
- `stream_done` resolves into `idle(Ready)` **or** `idle(Suspended)` (the done
  event carries the resolved chain state).
- New `accept` / `deny` / `cancel` events: `Suspended→Suspended` (partial) or
  `Suspended→Ready` (last resolve / cancel always).
- Rendering: `UnresolvedTool<T>`, `DeniedTool<T>`, `CancelledTool<T>` wrappers
  saved in-chain with their own renderers; Anthropic-style dialog replacing the
  input box, forcing resolve-all before a new message.

## Test plan (strong coverage of the state)

### Agent crate — pure transition (the heart of it)

- `derive_state`: all-resolved → `Ready`; one dangling → `Suspended[that]`;
  many dangling → `Suspended[all]`; no tool calls → `Ready`.
- `transition_suspended`:
  - accept-all → `Ready`, `resume=true`, results in correct positions
  - **accept-partial (k<n) → `Suspended[remaining]`, `resume=false`**
  - deny-one → `Suspended[remaining]`; deny-all → `Ready`, `resume=true`
  - mixed accept+deny covering all → `Ready`
  - cancel → all pending become `CancelledTool`, `Ready`, **`resume=false`**
  - **accept a user tool → placeholder appended, counts as resolved**
  - resolving an unknown / already-resolved `tool_call_id` → defined error / no-op
- detection: `destructiveHint=true` ends stream with dangling call;
  non-destructive executes; multi-call turn `[allow, gated, allow]` → allowed
  executed, gated dangling.
- `PermissionsRepo`: destructive → `NeedsPermission`, else `AlwaysAllow`.
- `resolve_pending_tool_calls`: permission-suspend leaves gated calls dangling;
  genuine cancel still synthesizes "cancelled".

### Frontend reducer (`chatState.ts`)

- `idle(Ready) + send` → `sending`; `idle(Suspended) + send` → rejected.
- `stream_done` → `idle(Ready)` vs `idle(Suspended)`.
- `accept/deny/cancel`: `Suspended→Suspended` (partial) and `Suspended→Ready`
  (last resolve / cancel).

## Key file paths

- Agent loop: `rust/cloud-storage/agent/src/agent_loop.rs`
- Tool trait / toolset: `rust/cloud-storage/ai_toolset/src/tool.rs`,
  `.../toolset/traits.rs`, `.../toolset/tool_object/user_tool.rs`
- DCS send endpoint (template): `document_cognition_service/src/api/stream/chat_message/mod.rs`
- Frontend chat state: `js/app/packages/core/component/AI/state/chatState.ts`
